Sisamai
siss-AH-may
n. (proper name; a man of the house of Jerahmeel in the genealogy of Judah)
Hebrew Sismay, of uncertain meaning. The name occurs twice, both in a single verse.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Sisamai is one link in a four-generation chain: “And Eleasah begat Sisamai, and Sisamai begat Shallum” (1 Chronicles 2:40), and the chain continues, “And Shallum begat Jekamiah, and Jekamiah begat Elishama” (1 Chronicles 2:41). The Authorized Version uses the name twice, both within the one verse, and nothing else is said of him. The dictionary notes what the passage is. 1 Chronicles 2 is the genealogy of Judah, written for a people just returned from Babylon who needed to know who they were — which families held which fields, which house was royal, which was priestly. The Chronicler works through Judah's sons, then Hezron, then Jerahmeel and Caleb, naming men nobody had heard of since before the exile. The purpose is restoration. A nation that has been deported for seventy years and comes home has to be able to prove its descent, and the register is how it does so. Sisamai is in the Bible because a returning Judahite needed to show his line, and God saw to it that the line was written down before the city fell.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) gives no entry for Sisamai; the name belongs to a man of the house of Jerahmeel in the genealogy of Judah.

Key Scripture

1Ch 2:40 — "And Eleasah begat Sisamai, and Sisamai begat Shallum,"

1Ch 2:41 — "And Shallum begat Jekamiah, and Jekamiah begat Elishama."

Ezr 2:62 — "These sought their register among those that were reckoned by genealogy, but they were not found: therefore were they, as polluted, put from the priesthood."

Modern Corruption

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition.

expand to see more

The nine chapters of genealogy at the head of Chronicles are the most skipped passage in the Old Testament, and the usual reason given is that they have no spiritual content. Ezra 2:62 shows what they were for: men who could not produce their register were put from the priesthood. A written descent was a legal necessity for a restored people, and the Chronicler supplied it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is God's provision before the need. The registers were written while the kingdom still stood; they were needed seventy years later by men who had been born in Babylon. He prepares the record before the exile that makes it necessary.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Sismay, of uncertain meaning; a Jerahmeelite in the Judahite genealogy of 1 Chronicles 2.

Hebrew Sismay; the meaning is not recoverable with certainty.

1 Chronicles 2:40 is the only verse in which the name occurs, twice.

He is son of Eleasah and father of Shallum.

The chain runs on to Jekamiah and Elishama in the next verse.

Ezra 2:62 shows why such registers mattered after the exile.
